Keywords and Getting Found

Where to Use Keywords on Pinterest

By Marie Glow StudioPublished August 3, 2026Updated September 26, 2026

Knowing your keywords isn't the hard part. Knowing exactly where they need to go is. On Pinterest, a keyword belongs in seven places: Pin titles, Pin descriptions, your profile name and bio, board titles and descriptions, image file names, alt text, and the title and headline of the page each Pin links to.

Where do keywords go on Pinterest?

Keywords go in seven places, from your profile to the page each Pin links to. Use this table as a checklist, then read the sections below for each row.

Pinterest keyword placement map
PlaceWhat to do there
Profile name and bioSay what you sell and who it is for, in words a customer would search.
Board titles and descriptionsName the topic plainly and describe what the board covers.
Pin titlesPut the main phrase first, not buried at the end.
Pin descriptionsWrite natural sentences that explain the Pin.
Image file namesRename the file before you upload it.
Alt textDescribe the image in plain words when your platform supports it.
Destination pageRepeat the promise in the page's title and headline.

What goes in your profile and board keywords?

Your profile name and bio should carry the phrase that describes your business, and each board title should carry the phrase for its topic. Think of the profile as the label on the front door and each board as a labeled shelf. A bio line such as “Pinterest SEO for handmade product businesses” states the subject and the reader it serves at once. A board description is a sentence or two on what the board holds, written for a person first.

If the profile is where you are stuck, the Pinterest profile SEO guide goes step by step, and Pinterest board SEO covers titles, descriptions and organization.

How do keywords work in Pin titles and descriptions?

Front-load the Pin title with its main phrase and write the description in natural sentences, not a keyword dump. Front-loading means the phrase comes first, so “Personalized birthday gift for a coworker” leads with the idea and does not save it for the last three words. The description then explains what the Pin shows and where the click leads, using related wording instead of repeating the same phrase.

Two guides go deeper: writing SEO-friendly Pin titles and writing Pinterest descriptions that get found.

Do image file names and alt text matter?

Yes, they are two quick places to add clarity. Rename the image file to a plain phrase before uploading, so it does not stay as a camera default like IMG_2041. Where your platform or theme supports alt text, add a short, honest description of what the image shows. A plain description, such as what is pictured and who it is for, works better than a list of search phrases.

Neither one replaces a good title or description. They simply make sure every piece of the Pin says the same thing.

Why should the destination page repeat the keyword?

Because the page's own title and headline are where the Pin's promise either carries through or falls apart. If a Pin says “handmade soy candle gift set” and the page headline says “Welcome to our shop”, the visitor has to work out whether they are in the right place. Matching the headline to the Pin lets the promise follow the click.

Check that the link goes to the most specific page, not the homepage, before you worry about anything else on this list.

How often should a keyword appear?

Use a phrase where it reads naturally and vary the wording elsewhere. A description that repeats one phrase four times reads like a list of search terms, and a person deciding whether to click will notice. Read the finished description once as if you had never seen your keyword list. If it flows, it is ready. Choose the primary phrase for each Pin first, using Pinterest keyword research, and if it feels too broad, make it more specific. The five step checklist for getting found puts these placements in a sensible order.

Placement is a review job first, and the plan tells you which of these to fix before the rest.

Frequently asked questions

Should I use the same keyword in every place on Pinterest?

No. Choose one main phrase for each Pin and place it in the Pin title, the description and the destination page, then let the wording vary in your profile, boards and image details. The placements should agree with one another without repeating the phrase word for word.

Do I need to rename image files before uploading them to Pinterest?

It is a quick step worth taking. Renaming the file to a plain descriptive phrase before you upload it keeps the image consistent with the Pin title and description around it.
